Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the Summit Insurance Group Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. Instructions for queuing your questions will be provided at that time. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Johnson: Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Summit Insurance Group's Q3 2024 earnings call. Joining me on the call today are Johnathan Hale, Chief Executive Officer; Michael Reynolds, Chief Financial Officer; Lisa Chen, Chief Underwriting Officer; and David Patel, Chief Investment Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we are making today may be considered forward-looking. These statements are subject to certain risks and uncertainties that could cause our actual results to differ materially from those projected. We encourage you to review our SEC filings for a more detailed discussion of these risks and uncertainties.

I will now turn the call over to Johnathan Hale.

Johnathan Hale: Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. I'm pleased to report on Summit Insurance Group's performance for Q3 2024. We delivered strong results, driven by robust premium growth, disciplined underwriting amid elevated catastrophe activity, effective reinsurance protections, favorable loss ratio improvements through targeted claims management, and strategic capital deployment into high-return opportunities. Our focus on advancing catastrophe modeling and diversifying exposures continues to yield positive outcomes, positioning us well for sustained profitability.

Michael, our CFO, will now provide a more detailed review of our financial performance.

Michael Reynolds: Thank you, Johnathan. Good morning, everyone. As Johnathan mentioned, we had a solid quarter. Our net income was $450 million, or $1.92 per share. Key drivers of our financial performance included premium expansion of 7.2%, operational efficiencies, and steady investment returns. Our combined ratio was 98.4%, reflecting effective underwriting and claims management despite catastrophe pressures. Investment income for the quarter was $620 million. We continue to maintain a strong capital position, with $15 billion in surplus capital and a risk-based capital ratio exceeding 550%.

As we dive deeper into our financial results, I'd like to spend some time on a critical metric for our industry: total catastrophe losses impact, expressed both in absolute dollar terms and as a percentage of gross written premiums, or GWP. Catastrophe losses remain a hallmark of property and casualty insurance volatility, driven by the intensifying frequency and severity of natural catastrophes amid climate change, secondary perils like severe convective storms, and socioeconomic factors like inflation-fueled rebuilding costs.

For the quarter ended September 30, 2024, our total catastrophe losses net of reinsurance recoveries came in at $1.2 billion, representing 4.8% of our GWP of $25.1 billion. This compares to $850 million, or 3.6% of GWP, in Q3 2023—a meaningful uptick year-over-year. On a nine-month rolling basis, year-to-date cat losses totaled $3.8 billion, or 4.2% of GWP, versus $2.9 billion and 3.3% last year. These figures are pre-tax and exclude any favorable prior-year development, which added $150 million to our bottom line this quarter.

Let me break this down by key drivers and regions to give you the full picture. North America accounted for 65% of our Q3 cat impact, or $780 million. The standout event was Hurricane Helene, which made landfall in the Florida Panhandle in late September as a Category 4 storm with $50 billion in insured losses industry-wide, per estimates from Verisk Analytics and PCS. Our personal lines property book in the Southeast U.S.—Florida, Georgia, and the Carolinas—bore the brunt, with gross losses of $950 million before a robust 55% cession to our catastrophe excess-of-loss reinsurance tower. This included $400 million from windstorm damage to coastal exposures and $200 million from inland flooding, exacerbated by storm surge and riverine overflow.

Complementing Helene were California wildfires, which contributed $250 million in Q3 losses. The Line Fire and Bridge Fire complexes scorched over 150,000 acres in Riverside and Los Angeles counties, mirroring the destructive patterns we've seen since the 2017-2021 fire seasons. Our commercial property portfolio here, underwritten through our Summit West division, saw elevated claims due to hardened wildfire exposure—think high-value assets in the wildland-urban interface. We've been proactive: post-2023's Maui and Hawaiian fires, we implemented stricter mitigation credits, reducing our probable maximum loss, or PML, by 15% in high-hazard zones via roof retrofits and defensible space requirements.

Internationally, Europe delivered $280 million in cat losses, or 2.1% of regional GWP, primarily from Storm Boris—a sprawling low-pressure system that dumped 300mm of rain across Central Europe in mid-September, rivaling the 2021 Ahr Valley floods. Germany, Poland, and the Czech Republic saw $18 billion in economic damages, with our motor and property lines hit for flood and wind claims. Our European motor book, which grew 12% year-over-year on rate and volume, benefited from parametric triggers in our reinsurance program, recovering 40% swiftly. Asia-Pacific added $140 million, driven by Typhoon Yagi's wrath in Vietnam and the Philippines—$10 billion industry loss event—impacting our micro-insurance partnerships with local carriers like Prudential and Manulife.

To put this in context, our all-cat combined operating ratio, or COR, for Q3 was 112.5%, versus 108.2% last year, with cats pushing the overall COR to 98.4%—still within our 95% target corridor despite the pressure. Attritional losses held steady at 62% of premiums earned, underscoring the discipline in our core underwriting. Reinsurance played a starring role: our $2.5 billion cat XOL program, renewed January 1 at a 10% lower cost thanks to improved modeled return periods, covered 75% of gross losses above $500 million per event, with no collateral calls triggered.

Now, on trends: Over the past five years, our cat losses as a percentage of GWP have trended up from 2.8% in 2020 to 4.2% year-to-date, aligning with industry benchmarks from AM Best and S&P, where global nat-cat insured losses hit $110 billion through Q3 per Munich Re's sigma reports. Key amplifiers include climate persistence, with secondary perils like U.S. derecho winds and hail—up 20% in frequency per RMS models—now rivaling tropical cyclones; inflation and exposure growth, where replacement costs are 25% higher than 2022 peaks per CoreLogic data, while our U.S. property book grew 8% year-over-year on rate adequacy; and social inflation, with litigation funding in wildfire claims inflating settlements by 15-20%.

Strategically, we're not sitting idle. Our catastrophe modeling has evolved with Summit CatRisk 2.0, our proprietary platform integrating AI-driven ensemble models from AIR Worldwide, RMS, and Karen Clark & Company. This incorporates stochastic event sets for compound risks—like hurricane plus flood—and climate projections to 2050, shaving 10% off our tail VaR at 99.5%. We've optimized our portfolio: U.S. Southeast gross exposure down 7% via non-renewals in Miami-Dade and Broward counties, redirecting to lower-volatility Midwest personal auto. Rate initiatives delivered 11.2% increases in property lines, outpacing loss trends, while our index-linked securities issuance of $500 million in June provides collateralized cat protection.

Regionally, we're diversifying: Asia growth via crop insurance partnerships in India, leveraging satellite imagery for monsoon perils, and EMEA expansion in cyber-physical hybrids—cats bundled with parametric cyber covers. Our 2025 reinsurance renewal targets a 5-7% cost reduction through swing layer optimizations and sidecars with third-party capital from Apollo and RenaissanceRe.

Looking forward, Q4 guidance pencils cat losses at 3.0-3.5% of GWP, assuming normalized Atlantic activity per NOAA's 18 named storms outlook. Active season risks like Milton persist, but our $1.8 billion risk corridor and $400 million cat bond outstanding provide ample buffer. Ultimate losses on Helene will finalize in Q1 2025, but early indicators suggest favorable development.

Turning now to our core underwriting performance, specifically loss ratio trends and the key drivers behind them—claims frequency and severity. I'll break this down by segment, region, and underlying factors, while highlighting the technical and strategic levers we're pulling to sustain our margin discipline in a volatile P&C environment.

Starting with the headline: Our consolidated calendar-year loss ratio for Q3 came in at 62.5%, a 270 basis point improvement from 65.2% in Q3 2023, and down 110 basis points sequentially from Q2 2024. This marks our best quarterly loss ratio since Q1 2022, excluding pandemic distortions. For the first nine months of 2024, we're at 63.8%, positioning us well toward our full-year guidance of 64-66%, ahead of the industry average of around 68% as reported by ISO and peer benchmarks from Travelers and Chubb.

This improvement wasn't accidental—it's the result of disciplined pricing, enhanced underwriting analytics, and proactive claims management amid persistent headwinds like social inflation and repair cost escalation.

Claims frequency trends were broadly stable to slightly favorable across most lines. In Personal Auto—our largest segment at 42% of earned premiums—frequency rose modestly by 2.8% year-over-year to 7.2 claims per 100 cars, driven by pent-up mobility post-COVID and a 4% uptick in miles driven per Verisk analytics. However, our telematics program, now penetrating 28% of our book (up from 22% last year), mitigated this through usage-based pricing; safe drivers saw 15% lower frequency rates.

In Homeowners, frequency was flat at 1.8 claims per 100 policies, but we absorbed a 12% year-over-year spike in weather-related claims from convective storms in the Midwest and Southeast—think derechos in Iowa and hail events in Texas, echoing patterns seen industry-wide with Swiss Re estimating $15 billion in U.S. severe convective storm losses year-to-date. Commercial Lines saw a slight 1.5% decline to 4.1 claims per 100 policies, benefiting from our small business focus where we've tightened workers' comp attachments.

Claims severity remains the bigger challenge, up 6.9% year-over-year on average to $18,400 per claim, fueled by three interlocking pressures: parts and labor inflation, medical cost trends, and litigation funding dynamics. Auto severity jumped 8.2% to $22,500 per claim, with OEM parts costs up 11% per CCC Intelligent Solutions data—supply chain snarls from the Red Sea disruptions haven't helped—and body shop labor rates hitting $55/hour in California markets. Liability severity in Commercial Auto was even hotter at +10.4%, exacerbated by social inflation; nuclear verdicts over $10 million are now 25% more common per Jury Verdict Research, mirroring Allstate's commentary on adverse jury trends.

Homeowners severity climbed 5.7% to $14,200, largely from water damage repairs amid aging housing stock, while property cat losses added 150 basis points to the ratio from Hurricane Helene's fringes in Florida and North Carolina—our gross cat losses totaled $220 million pretax, reinsured above our $100 million retention via our layered quota-share and excess-of-loss towers with partners like Swiss Re and RenaissanceRe.

By segment and region: Personal Lines (55% of premiums) posted a loss ratio of 64.2%, down 350 basis points year-over-year. Auto at 66.8% (improved via 9.5% earned rate hikes and 12% non-renewals in California), Homeowners at 59.1% (bolstered by roof age restrictions and mitigation incentives).

Before moving on, I'd like to highlight the effectiveness of our reinsurance program, which continues to be a cornerstone of our risk management strategy. In an environment marked by escalating catastrophe losses—think Hurricane Idalia's $50 billion industry-wide impact last year and the ongoing wildfire seasons in California—our reinsurance placements have delivered exceptional protection, optimizing capital efficiency and supporting our mid-teens ROE targets.

For the full year to date through Q3, our gross written premiums reached $25.1 billion, up 8% year-over-year, driven by strong P&C growth in our commercial lines. We ceded approximately 22% of gross premiums, or $5.5 billion, to our reinsurance partners—a slight dip from 24% last year, reflecting our disciplined retention strategy amid a softening reinsurance market. This cession rate strikes the optimal balance: high enough to cap our net probable maximum loss, or PML, at under 5% of surplus on a 1-in-100-year event across our portfolio, per our updated RMS v18 cat modeling runs, while preserving attractive ceding commissions averaging 28% on our quota share treaties.

On recoveries, we've seen outstanding performance. Year-to-date, reinsurance recoverables stand at $2.8 billion, representing a 92% recovery rate on paid losses exceeding our retention layers. Take our excess-of-loss program for U.S. Northeast winter storms and Gulf hurricanes: during the active 2024 Atlantic season, we triggered $450 million in gross cat losses from Helene and Milton analogs, but net retention was just $120 million after reinsurance—a 73% risk transfer. This compares favorably to peers like Chubb or Travelers, who reported higher net hits in their Q2 calls due to tighter layers. Our loss ratio pre-reinsurance was 68%, but post-reinsurance, it improved to 52%, directly contributing 450 basis points to our accident year combined ratio of 92.1%—well below our 95% target.

Trend-wise, we've navigated the reinsurance cycle masterfully. Coming off the 2023 hardening—where rates spiked 25-40% on Florida wind and California fire layers—we locked in multi-year programs at the January 1 renewals, securing a 7% reduction in net cost year-over-year. Pricing on our proportional treaties is now stable at 85-90% of gross, with collateral requirements down to 15% thanks to our A+ rated panel. We've also layered in innovative structures: 15% of our cat tower is now backed by insurance-linked securities, or ILS, via catastrophe bonds issued through our Bermuda SPV, yielding mid-single-digit returns while diversifying away from traditional reinsurers. This ILS allocation, up from 8% in 2023, performed flawlessly during the European floods earlier this year, recovering $180 million with zero collateral calls.

Regionally, our program shines. In North America, which accounts for 55% of our book, we've optimized Florida exposure post-SB 2A reforms—reducing our net coastal retention by 20% through higher excess points with Swiss Re and Munich Re on our $500 million xs $50 million layers. Europe, at 25% of premiums, benefited from our flood quota share with Hannover Re, ceding 35% of gross and recovering 95% of the $300 million in Storm Babet losses. Asia-Pacific, our fastest-growing region at 12% year-over-year, leverages typhoon excess covers with PartnerRe, capping net losses at 2% of surplus despite record intensities—think Typhoon Yagi's $20 billion footprint.

Strategically, we're not standing still. We've invested $15 million in advanced analytics, integrating Guy Carpenter's Quantum modeling with our proprietary ML-driven exposure accumulation tools, which flagged and mitigated $200 million in over-concentrated California brush risk pre-renewal. This tech edge allowed us to negotiate 10-15% better terms, including reinstatement premiums capped at 50% and commutation options after three loss-free years. Looking forward, we're exploring sidecars with Berkshire Hathaway for our E&S lines, targeting $500 million in additional capacity at low cost, while embedding ESG overlays—prioritizing reinsurers with strong TCFD disclosures to align with our net-zero by 2040 commitment.

As we wrap up our results, I'd like to turn to our capital deployment strategy, which remains a cornerstone of delivering superior shareholder returns in this dynamic insurance landscape. We ended the quarter with a robust $4.8 billion in deployable excess capital, up 12% year-over-year, bolstered by our industry-leading 95.2% combined ratio and $2.1 billion in net investment income—driven by higher reinvestment yields at 4.8% amid the Fed's steady rate environment. Our risk-based capital ratio stands at a pristine 620%, well above regulatory thresholds and our internal 500% target, giving us ample dry powder to execute opportunistically.

Our capital allocation framework prioritizes three pillars: (1) high-return organic investments, (2) disciplined inorganic growth through bolt-on acquisitions, and (3) consistent shareholder returns via dividends and buybacks. We target a 12-15% ROE over the cycle, and we're on track, with trailing 12-month ROE at 14.2%.

First, organic growth through new products and capabilities. We're laser-focused on adjacency expansion in property & casualty, where we see embedded growth potential amid escalating risks like cyber threats and climate volatility. In Q3, we launched Summit CyberShield Pro, a parametric cyber insurance product tailored for mid-market enterprises, leveraging AI-driven threat modeling from our partnership with CrowdStrike. This builds on our $250 million tech investment last year in machine learning underwriting engines, which have already reduced loss ratios by 180 basis points in our commercial lines to 62.4%. Early traction is strong: CyberShield Pro has generated $180 million in gross written premiums run-rate annualized, with a projected 25% attach rate to our existing D&O and E&O portfolios. We expect this suite to contribute 8-10% to our overall P&C premium growth in 2025, targeting $1.2 billion in new premiums.

On the personal lines front, we're rolling out EV Guardian, a usage-based auto product integrating telematics with our Snapshot app—similar to Progressive's model but enhanced with EV-specific battery degradation coverage. With U.S. EV penetration hitting 9% this year per Cox Automotive data, we're pricing for a 15% rate adequacy adjustment to offset higher repair costs, which have surged 22% year-over-year. Regionally, this is U.S.-centric initially, but we're adapting it for Europe via our Lloyd's syndicate, where EV adoption is at 14% and regulatory pressures under the EU Green Deal demand tailored products.

In life and health, we're addressing longevity risk with Summit Longevity Flex, a hybrid annuity-variable universal life product incorporating ESG-linked riders. This taps into the $4 trillion U.S. retirement savings gap, per LIMRA estimates, and we've seeded it with $500 million in assets under management already, pricing for a 105% crediting rate floor amid 10-year Treasury yields at 4.3%.

These initiatives are underpinned by technical investments: $300 million committed this year to cloud-native claims platforms using generative AI from our Palantir collaboration, aiming to cut claims cycle times by 40% and expense ratios to under 28%. We've also piloted blockchain for reinsurance contracts, reducing disputes by 30% in our retrocession book.

Second, inorganic growth via acquisitions. M&A remains a high-conviction lever, especially tuck-ins in underserved niches where we can deploy our float advantage—our $45 billion investment portfolio yields a stable 4.2% book yield. We've allocated $2-3 billion for 2024-2025 deals, targeting 10-12% IRR thresholds post-synergies.

In Q4, we're closing our $1.1 billion acquisition of Pacific Specialty Lines, a West Coast specialty carrier with $800 million in GWP focused on earthquake and wildfire parametric triggers—critical given California's 2024 catastrophe losses exceeding $15 billion, per PCS data. This deal accretes 50 cents to book value immediately and expands our West Coast market share from 4% to 7%, with 200 basis points of expense synergies from our shared services platform.

Looking ahead, we're actively pursuing opportunities in Asia-Pacific, where premium growth is outpacing the U.S. at 7.2% CAGR through 2028 (Swiss Re sigma). We've shortlisted targets like a Singapore-based cyber reinsurer and an Indian health micro-insurer, akin to Chubb's Huatai stake, to capture the $100 billion untapped protection gap. In Europe, post-Brexit consolidation favors us; we're eyeing a UK motor pool to bolster our 12% combined ratio there amid softening rates.

We've passed on larger deals like the rumored Allianz-HCSC talks, sticking to our "barbell" strategy: small-to-mid bolt-ons ($500 million-$2 billion) alongside organic bets, avoiding the integration risks seen in OneMain's property casualty foray.

Finally, shareholder returns. With 60% of deployable capital earmarked for growth, the balance flows back to you. We've raised our quarterly dividend 8% to $0.65 per share, yielding 2.4% forward, and authorized a $1.5 billion share repurchase—deploying $750 million year-to-date at an average 18% discount to book value. This supports our goal of 10% annual EPS growth, excluding catastrophes.

As we turn to our forward-looking guidance, I'd like to provide a detailed update on our premium growth outlook for Q4 2024 and the full fiscal year 2025. Our guidance reflects a disciplined approach to underwriting profitability amid a gradually softening P&C market, continued rate momentum in select lines, and our strategic investments in data analytics and digital distribution.

Starting with the headline numbers: We are guiding for net written premium growth of 6% to 8% in Q4 2024, sequentially building on our Q3 actual of 7.2%. For the full year 2025, we expect premium growth in the 9% to 11% range, up from our prior guide of 8% to 10%, driven by stronger-than-expected new business wins and retention in our high-margin commercial segments. This positions us at the upper end of industry peers like Travelers and Chubb, who recently guided mid-single digits for 2025 amid similar catastrophe normalization.

By line of business, personal lines will contribute the lion's share early on. In homeowners and dwelling fire, we're projecting 10% to 12% growth in Q4, fueled by 5.5% average rate increases approved across 42 states—including California, where we've successfully navigated the FAIR Plan surcharge environment post-wildfire season—and a 92% policy retention rate, up 150 basis points year-over-year. Volume growth here is supported by our expanded telematics partnerships with Progressive-like usage-based programs, now covering 1.2 million policies and delivering 15% better loss ratios through granular risk selection.

Personal auto remains a modest grower at 4% to 6% for Q4 and 7% to 9% in 2025, reflecting rate discipline of 4.2% nationally despite competitive pressures from direct writers like Geico. Our edge comes from AI-driven underwriting models, which have reduced adverse selection by 8% via real-time MVR and claims history integration, enabling us to capture 2 million incremental policies through embedded insurance APIs with auto OEMs like Ford and GM.

Commercial lines are our growth engine, with 12% to 15% expansion expected across the board. Middle-market property expects 14% growth, leveraging 6.8% rate hikes and a 15% increase in new business submissions from our Summit Business Shield platform—a cyber-physical bundled product that's gained traction amid rising ransomware attacks, similar to Allianz's offerings. Workers' comp will see 10% growth, benefiting from payroll inflation pass-throughs and our OSHA-compliant safety telematics for construction clients, which have lowered ex-mod rates by 20% on average. In specialty lines like D&O and E&S, we're targeting 18% growth in 2025, capitalizing on the hard market's tailwinds before capacity floods in from Lloyd's and Bermuda reinsurers.

Regionally, North America drives 70% of our premium base and 10% growth in 2025, with the U.S. Southeast and Midwest outperforming at 12% due to hurricane recovery rebuilds and industrial expansion. California remains challenged at 5% growth, constrained by Prop 103 rate filing delays and wildfire exposure, but our catastrophe XL tower—reinsured at 95% quota share with Swiss Re—mitigates tail risk. Europe, 20% of premiums, guides to 7% growth, tempered by Solvency II capital charges but boosted by 8% rate gains in UK motor following the Ogden discount rate reset. Our Asia-Pacific expansion, now 10% of the book via the 2023 acquisition of a regional P&C arm, targets 15% to 18% growth, focusing on micro-insurance products for gig economy workers in Indonesia and Vietnam, akin to Ping An's model.

Key strategic initiatives underpinning this guidance include our $250 million 'Summit NextGen' tech stack rollout, live in 80% of agencies by Q1 2025. This integrates predictive analytics from Google Cloud and Verisk's catastrophe models to optimize pricing grids, targeting a 200 basis point improvement in our 92.5% Q3 combined ratio. We're also doubling down on broker partnerships, with new flows from Aon and Marsh up 25%, and launching parametric triggers for flood and wildfire in high-risk zones—a product innovation mirroring Lemonade's tech-forward approach but scaled for enterprise.

Of course, risks to this guidance include elevated cat activity—we've baked in $400 million of normalized losses for 2025, versus $350 million actual year-to-date—persistent medical inflation in comp lines (projected at 5.5%), and softening rates if capacity from ILS funds like Twelve Capital oversupplies the market. That said, our 98% reinsurance recoverables and A+ AM Best rating provide a strong buffer.

In summary, while Q3 cats tested us, our resilient balance sheet and underwriting discipline position Summit for mid-teens ROEs. Our capital deployment is calibrated for a hardening market: cyber premiums up 25% industry-wide, climate products growing 30% per McKinsey, and interest tailwinds persisting. We're positioned to compound book value per share at 11-13% annually, outpacing peers like Travelers (9%) and even Berkshire's insurance ops. Our 6-8% Q4 and 9-11% FY25 premium growth guidance reflects robust fundamentals: rate adequacy, superior retention, and tech-enabled expansion. This supports our EPS outlook of $8.50 to $9.00 for 2025, with ROE north of 15%. Our reinsurance program isn't just effective—it's a competitive moat, delivering $600 million in capital relief this year alone and positioning us to deploy $1.2 billion in organic growth without compromising our AA- ratings.

Lisa Chen: Thank you, Michael. I'd like to provide an update on our underwriting performance. We've seen continued strong performance in our commercial lines segment. We are actively managing our exposure to catastrophe-prone regions like the U.S. Southeast and California wildfires and have implemented several initiatives to improve our risk selection, including AI-enhanced modeling and stricter mitigation requirements, which have helped stabilize our attritional loss ratios.

Operator, we are now ready to open the line for questions.

Operator: Thank you. Instructions for submitting questions: Press star then one on your touchtone phone. Our first question comes from John Smith with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

John Smith: Good morning. Can you provide more color on the outlook for catastrophe losses into Q4 and 2025, especially with the active hurricane season?

Johnathan Hale: Good morning, John. As Michael outlined, we're guiding Q4 cat losses at 3.0-3.5% of GWP, assuming normalized activity per NOAA. We've got strong buffers from our $1.8 billion risk corridor and cat bonds, and our portfolio optimizations—like Southeast non-renewals—have reduced PMLs meaningfully.

Operator: Our next question comes from Emily Carter with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Emily Carter: Good morning. Could you discuss the impact of recent interest rate stability on your investment portfolio and capital deployment?

Michael Reynolds: Good morning, Emily. Higher reinvestment yields at 4.8% have boosted our $620 million quarterly investment income, supporting $4.8 billion in deployable capital. We're prioritizing organic products like CyberShield Pro and tuck-in M&As like Pacific Specialty, while returning capital via buybacks and an 8% dividend hike.

Operator: Our next question comes from David Lee with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

David Lee: What is the expected impact of potential regulatory changes in California on your underwriting strategy?

Lisa Chen: Good morning, David. California remains challenging with Prop 103 delays, but our reinsurance—95% quota share on XL towers—and mitigation credits have kept growth at 5%, with loss ratios improving via non-renewals and telematics. We're adapting with parametric wildfire products.

Operator: Our next question comes from Rachel Kim with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Rachel Kim: Thanks. On premium growth guidance, how confident are you in the 9-11% for 2025, given softening markets?

Michael Reynolds: High confidence, Rachel. Commercial lines at 12-15% drive it, with tech like NextGen analytics and broker flows from Aon up 25%. Retention at 92% and rate hikes outpace inflation, even baking in cat normalization.

Operator: Seeing no further questions at this time...

Johnathan Hale: Thank you for your questions and your interest in Summit Insurance Group. In closing, we are confident in our ability to continue delivering strong results and creating value for our shareholders. Thank you for joining us today.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
